refutes.claim: None of the visible hunks touch how `SuppressSourceGeneration` is handled. The type-collector changes only add `continue` after the mixed-key MsgPack005 report and replace `Dictionary.Add` with a `ContainsKey` guard. Both avoid an analyzer crash for every type, suppressed or not. If the 3.1.1 regression is that types with `SuppressSourceGeneration = true` are skipped by the analyzer, then plain violations still go unreported. An example is a missing `[Key]` (MsgPack004) on a well-formed suppressed type. In that case the first acceptance criterion is not met. Only the crash paths would be fixed.

title: Receipts/DuplicateKeySilentlyDroppedTests.cs: edge-case test passes on head (2 tests): no defect shown; refutes 2 lens claim(s): logic-edge-1, logic-edge-2

refutes.claim: The new `ContainsKey` guards turn a duplicate `[Key]` into silent first-wins with no diagnostic. Example input: a `[MessagePackObject]` with `[Key(0)] public int FirstValue` and `[Key(0)] public int SecondValue`, or the same string key on two members. On base, `Dictionary.Add` threw, so the problem surfaced as AD0001 or CS8785. On head nothing is reported. With generation not suppressed, the generated formatter serializes only `FirstValue` and silently drops `SecondValue`, so data is lost on round-trip. The dynamic resolver rejects duplicate keys at run time, so the analyzer now hides an error it used to surface. This also changes behaviour when `SuppressSourceGeneration` is unset, which the requirement says must not change.

The same silent first-wins guard was added to the string-key path in the second member-collection loop (the field/constructor variant at the 1145-1180 region). A duplicate string key there is dropped without any diagnostic. In map mode the later member, for example a derived `new` member that hides a base member with the same key, is silently not serialized, depending on member enumeration order.
